description: We are a team of sophomore Mechanical Engineering students at Nile University, Egypt, driven by curiosity and a passion for engineering innovation. Our interests span space exploration, EV battery design, robotics, embedded systems, automation, and mathematical modeling. We enjoy exploring ideas beyond our disciplines, connecting engineering concepts with scientific discoveries, and turning complex challenges into creative, practical solutions.
summary:
Lunavista is an interactive lunar mission-planning prototype designed to make selecting and comparing Moon landing locations more accessible and understandable.

The platform combines a NASA-derived 3D Moon model, historical lunar landing sites, candidate landing regions, and configurable mission requirements. Users can explore how different mission architectures, spacecraft, crew sizes, power demands, communication needs, and science-versus-engineering priorities influence landing-site evaluation.

A distinctive feature is our Lunar DNA concept, which represents mission requirements and environmental conditions as comparable patterns. Lunavista also introduces crew-aware planning scenarios and a See Why explanation that helps users understand the factors behind a selection.

The current prototype demonstrates interactive exploration, mission configuration, and educational decision support. Future development will integrate validated time-dependent illumination, terrain, and communication calculations using NASA data.

Our goal is to make lunar landing decisions easier to explore, compare, explain, and communicate between scientists, engineers, students, and the public.
details:
LUNAVISTA — Lunar Mission Decision System

Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
Event: 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge — Cairo

The Problem

Selecting a lunar landing site is not simply about finding a flat surface. Mission planners must consider sunlight for solar power, Earth visibility for communications, terrain conditions, scientific opportunities, spacecraft limitations, and—in crewed missions—human operational requirements.

These factors can conflict. A location that offers significant scientific value may also present challenges for energy availability, communication, or astronaut activities. Changes in mission dates or spacecraft requirements can further complicate the decision.

Our Solution

Lunavista is an interactive web-based lunar mission decision-support prototype that allows users to explore landing locations, configure a mission, examine operational trade-offs, and understand the factors that influence site selection.

The prototype combines five main elements:

1. Interactive Lunar Atlas

Users explore a 3D Moon visualization based on NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter resources. The atlas includes historical crewed and robotic mission locations alongside candidate landing regions. Users can navigate the globe, inspect coordinates, and select locations for further investigation.

2. Mission Configuration

The interface allows users to select robotic, crewed, or combined crewed–robotic missions; choose from relevant launch-vehicle configurations; specify mission dates, duration, crew size, and operational requirements; and explore how these selections change the mission scenario.

3. Lunar DNA and Crew-Aware Planning

Our Lunar DNA concept represents mission requirements as a structured operating profile, including energy, communication, workload, and crew-related constraints.

For crewed missions, users can select historical lunar travelers and experiment with explicitly fictional health and performance scenarios. These include metabolic heat generation, cooling capacity, EVA duration, and thermal sensitivity. This demonstrates why different operational requirements may favor different lunar environments.

The medical parameters are educational assumptions, not actual medical records or assessments of named astronauts.

4. Science vs. Engineering Trade-off

An interactive slider demonstrates the competing priorities of scientific exploration and engineering reliability. Users can adjust these priorities to understand how mission preferences influence decisions.

Mandatory safety and feasibility requirements should not be overridden by preference weights.

5. Explainable Decision Support — “See Why This Site?”

Instead of presenting an unexplained recommendation, Lunavista provides a numbered explanation addressing mission architecture, spacecraft, terrain, sunlight, communication, crew considerations, operational workload, scientific priorities, and missing evidence.

It also compares fictional environmental scenarios to illustrate how changing requirements can affect suitability.

Implementation

The prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for browser-based 3D interaction. It incorporates NASA lunar visualization resources, historical mission information, interactive forms, custom filtering, and scenario-based decision explanations.

The application is intended to run directly in a modern web browser without specialist software.

Current Capabilities

The implemented prototype includes interactive mission setup, a lunar location catalog, a NASA 3D model loading interface, configurable crew scenarios, a science–engineering priority slider, and an explanation panel. The crew and environmental comparisons use educational simulation values.

Current Limitations

Lunavista is not a flight-certified mission-planning tool. It does not yet perform fully validated, terrain-aware Sun and Earth visibility calculations for every selected site and date. The site comparisons do not prove actual landing safety, and historical location markers may use approximate coordinates.

The high-resolution NASA 3D model may require a separate download or manual loading in some browsers.

Future Development

We aim to integrate JPL Horizons ephemerides, high-resolution LOLA/LROC terrain data, local horizon calculations, solar-power estimation, direct-to-Earth communication-window prediction, improved uncertainty analysis, and validated mission-constraint checking.

We also envision extending Lunar DNA into a time-dependent environment-matching engine and developing an “Ask the Moon” system that identifies which missing observations would most improve a landing decision.

Impact

Lunavista aims to bridge the gap between complex lunar datasets and understandable mission decisions. It can support early-stage mission concept exploration, communication between science and engineering teams, and education about the challenges of lunar exploration.

Our central principle is simple: selecting a landing site should involve not just identifying a location, but understanding why it may—or may not—fit the mission.
